blocks.text: The study protocol and amendments (Section 16.1.1) and informed consent form (ICF) (Section 16.1.3.2) were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB)/Independent Ethics Committee (IEC) at each participating site. A list of all IRBs/IECs used in this study is provided in Section 16.1.3.1.
container_path: 5.1. Independent Ethics Committee or Institutional Review Board

blocks.text: 5.2. Ethical Conduct of the Study

The study was conducted in accordance with Good Clinical Practice (GCP) as required by the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) guidelines and the FDA. Compliance with these requirements also constitutes conformity with the US 21 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 50 (Protection of Human Subjects), US 21 Part 56 (Institutional Review Boards), ICH Harmonised Tripartite Guideline, Guideline for GCP E6(R1), the Nuremburg Code, and the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
5.3. Subject Information and Consent

Copies of the IRB-approved Informed Consent Form (ICF) were received and reviewed by Histogenics Corporation (Sponsor) prior to the enrollment of patients at an investigational site. The ICF document approved by the site's IRB was signed by the patient and the Investigator prior to enrollment. The Investigator provided a copy of the signed ICF to the patient, and the original was retained by the Investigator. A sample ICF is provided in Section 16.1.3.2.
6. INVESTIGATORS AND STUDY ADMINISTRATIVE STRUCTURE

The study was a multi-national, multi-center study conducted in 30 centers in the United States (US) and in 3 centers in Canada. Fourteen (14) additional centers in the US and one in Canada. were initiated but did not enroll any patients. Of these 5 consented one or more patients that screen failed (never randomized). The lists of all Investigators and other key study personnel, with their affiliations, a description of their role in the study, and their qualifications, are provided in Section 16.1.4.1, with copies of their curricula vitae where relevant (Section 16.1.4.2). Investigators were trained at site initiation visits. Signed approval of the report from the Principal Investigator and the Sponsor's responsible medical officer is provided in Section 16.1.5. The study administrative structure is described in Table 1.

7. INTRODUCTION

Cartilage is the specialized fibrous connective tissue of primarily mesenchymal origin that forms the skeleton of the human body during development that is replaced with bone. Mature cartilage forming cells (chondrocytes) secrete the components of the extracellular matrix (hyaluronan, chondroitin sulfates and keratan sulfate) and tropocollagen, which polymerizes extracellularly into fine collagen fibers. Cartilage persists in the growing fetus, throughout development and into adulthood in further differentiated forms. The three most common are articular hyaline, elastic and fibrocartilage. Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage that covers the surface of bones at the joint space acting as a shock absorber and enabling the bones to glide over each other with minimal friction. Articular cartilage is covered by the synovial membrane which secretes the non-Newtonian synovial fluid that keeps the joint lubricated. Damage to the articular cartilage may be due to acute injury or repetitive trauma, and patients often experience pain and loss of function for several years due to the lack of efficacious medical treatments.

The existence of a cartilage defect in the knee joint is an important clinical finding since full thickness defects do not heal spontaneously once skeletal maturity is reached (Chalmers, 2013) and can result in debilitating symptoms such as pain, swelling, catching and grinding with knee movement (Bhosale and Richardson, 2008). Although chondrocytes produce matrix components throughout life, their production is unable to keep pace with the repair requirements after acute damage to hyaline cartilage. If cartilage is injured after a period of active growth, the defects are usually filled by connective tissue or fibrous cartilage. The extracellular matrix of these repair tissues is only poorly integrated with the matrix of the damaged cartilage. In addition, these types of repair tissue have less resiliency than mature articular cartilage. Left untreated, such lesions may progress to degenerative osteoarthritis (Buckwalter and Mankin, 1998), which is the third leading cause of work disability in adult populations in the United States (Theis et al., 2017). By extension, disability and the often-associated opioid addiction crisis is an enormous contributor to the annual pharmacoeconomic burden and medical costs to society. The ultimate goal of treatment of cartilage injuries in the knee is for clinicians to be able to restore joint function to pre-injury levels in a timely, predictable and durable fashion.

There is a significant unmet medical need for knee cartilage defects resulting in symptoms of pain and reduced function. Although treatment options for cartilage defects in the knee have evolved over the past 25 years, there remains a need for predictable and durable treatments. With current surgical strategies, many patients remain symptomatic, or symptoms return within one to two years of the intervention. In the United States, based on reimbursement codes demonstrating incidence, it is believed that approximately 1.2 million patients each year have arthroscopies where focal cartilage defects are identified. Only approximately 500,000 patients ultimately receive treatment with the large majority being debridement and microfracture (Mfx). Despite the limitations of microfracture, there are still approximately 150,000 microfracture procedures done each year.

Due to the variable outcomes of current treatment options including the prolonged rehabilitation phase, many patients elect to tolerate knee pain and loss of function with as many as 60% of patients avoiding or delaying treatment. These cartilage injuries, along with other knee injuries, are believed to be one of the primary predictors of later stage osteoarthritis. These injuries can have a significant economic impact for both the patient and the health care system with time lost from work, progression of disease and potential eventual need for joint replacement. Better treatment options are particularly important given the youngerdemographics of the affected individuals in their prime earning, sporting, or childraising years.

Clinical trials in the cartilage treatment space have been challenging to conduct due to patient perceptions regarding microfracture, difficult to recruit due to the specific inclusion / exclusion criteria for isolated defects, and until recent FDA guidance, lacked clarity on the appropriate endpoints for evaluation in clinical studies. Due to the paucity of adequate and well-controlled clinical studies in the United States, it is also difficult to make meaningful comparisons across treatment modalities.

The current treatment options can be broadly classified into three categories and are described in Table 2. Palliation (chondroplasty and debridement), repair (microfracture) or restorative (mosaicplasty, osteochondral auto or allograft, autologous chondrocyte implantation). While all have demonstrated benefit, especially in specific patient populations, there are many limitations and clinicans and patients have sought a better solution across the range of lesion sizes and body types.

blocks.text: 7.1. Repairative Treatments

While chondroplasty and debridement can alleviate pain for some period of time by trimming and smoothing damaged cartilage in the knee, they are not curative procedures. The area of damaged cartilage is unable to regenerate and create a smooth hyaline covered joint. This limitation is what led

Page 15 of 138

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

attempts to either allow the body to self repair the defect or provide the necessary cells to replace the missing cartilage and integrate into the patient's native knee cartilage. These methods have been met with varying degrees of success. While all of the treatment options are perceived as less than ideal, industry and the FDA sought to determine the most appropriate control arm for clinical development. Debridement does not treat the underlying defect, and auto/allograft tissue results are variable and not consistently available. Microfracture had become the standard of care starting approximately 20 years ago, particularly for smaller lesions, and protocols were developed to provide for a fair basis of comparison to this repair procedure.
7.2. Microfracture

In 1997, Steadman, et al., introduced the concept of "microfracture" as a reparative approach to chondral defects [8]. As originally performed, the focal defect is debrided until the subchondral bone plate is visualized. Using an arthroscopic awl, a series of holes 3-4 mm apart are created (with 3 to 4 holes/cm2) such that bone marrow is released to create a fibrin clot filled with endogenous reparative-stimulating agents (e.g., mesenchymal stem cells, growth factors, and cell-signaling proteins). Mesenchymal stem cells within the clot begin to proliferate, and several weeks after the procedure, cell differentiation creates cells that histologically appear similar to cartilage progenitor cells [9]. As time elapses (in terms of months and years), fibrocartilage - not hyaline cartilage - comprises most of the former defect.

During the initial post-procedure timeframe, the clot may become dislodged leading to early failure. To prevent this, patients must be non-weightbearing for a minimum of 6 weeks and then slowly progress to increased activity over the next 6 to 8 months with high impact activities and sports initiated after the 1- year mark. This Steadman defined rehabilitation protocol is deemed to be critically important - this slow progression and the strict adherence to a rehabilitation protocol is essential for success of the procedure and yet in reality can be difficult for patients to maintain given the normal demands of work and life. Such rehabilitation protocol was utilized in the NeoCart Phase III trial to ensure best possible outcomes with microfracture.

Unfortunately, even when proper rehabilitation is followed the clot may not heal or it may heal with soft fibrocartilage that lacks the resilience of articular cartilage. This accounts for the high failure rate often seen with microfracture starting 2 to 4 years after treatment and recent literature suggests that the failure rate at 5 years may be as high as 60%, with the median time of failure being at 4 years (Solheim, 2018).

Over the last 20 years, clinicans now recognize, however, that the quality of clinical outcomes after microfracture is dependent upon several variables. Proper patient selection, surgical technique, and regimented physical therapy/rehabilitation all affect clinical outcome and patient satisfaction; each of these factors are addressed below.
7.2.1. Patient selection and success factors

Mithoefer, et al., [10] conducted a meta-analysis to systematically examine the clinical efficacy of microfracture by identifying studies that featured short- and long-term functional outcome scores, macroscopic and microscopic cartilage repair quality, and results from postoperative MRI assessments. The researchers identified 28 studies describing 3122 patients. By integrating the results of these studies, the authors identified a series of factors that affect the clinical outcome after microfracture. Their table [10] is reproduced below (Table 3).

As seen above, assiduous patient selection is key to achieving positive outcomes after microfracture surgery. The researchers found, similar to the findings of Kreuz, et al. [11], that patients over 40 years of age tended to have worse outcomes than their younger counterparts. Lesions smaller than 4 cm2 were associated with better outcomes; the study by Kreuz, et al. [11] indicated that defects >2 cm2 tended to have worse outcomes, thus tightening their criteria for optimal patients. In this regard, a meta-analysis of Goyal, et al. [12] agrees with both groups of previously cited researchers: in their study, good clinical outcomes were associated with small lesions in younger patients with low post-operative demands.

In a 2016 review paper, Sommerfeldt, et al. [13], describe characteristics of a patient most likely to benefit from the microfracture procedure, "it [microfracture] is more likely to be successful when performed as a primary procedure for nonobese patients under the age of thirty to forty years with small (<2 to 4-cm2) femoral condylar defects that have been symptomatic for a short time (less than twelve to twenty-four months)."

blocks.text: 7.2.2. Microfracture Surgical Technique

The underlying principle of microfracture is to access the pluripotent mesenchymal stem cells present in bone marrow - found just under subchondral bone - in order to stimulate the repair of cartilage defects. The goal, then, is to optimize the availability of these reparative cells within the defect. The techniques developed to achieve this goal are immensely varied: hole spacing (density), hole depth, method of hole creation (awls vs. drills), whether or not to create holes (and risk structural damage to subchondral bone). Chen, et al. [14], examined the creation of holes via compaction (i.e., micro-"fracture" via awls) vs. water-cooled drilling and the role of hole depth. Four micro-holes were created in the trochlear groove of New Zealand white rabbits: 1 hole ~2 mm in depth was created using an awl, 2 holes created by a drill to a depth of ~2 mm and the remaining hole drilled to a depth of~6 mm; these series of 4 holes were replicated bilaterally in a total of 2 rabbits. The rabbits were sacrificed at 24 hours and the subchondral surfaces were examined histologically. The authors found that the compaction of bone using an awl created channels with restricted blood egress due residual bony remnants. The drilled channels were free of bony remnants and provided patent holes for blood egress. The authors had expected to find that drilling would create thermal necrosis in nearby osteocytes, but this did not occur. Surprisingly, they found disruption of nearby osteophytes during compaction, which they attributed to high shear forces created during the microfracture process. They concluded that the creation of microchannels via drilling was preferred over the use of awls in order to create patent holes that would encourage the flow of pluripotent cells.

While microfracture technique likely influences functional outcomes, a study by Kroell, et al. [15] demonstrates the difficulty in achieving uniformity of technique. In their research, the authors instruct four surgeons to create microfracture holes of a prescribed depth and density (i.e., spacing) in six pre-

Page 17 of 138

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

prepared chondral defects in fresh cadaveric knees. They observed, "all surgeons misjudged depth and inter-hole distance tending to make microfracture holes too deep (depth error 1.1 mm + 1.9) and too close together (inter-hole distance error: - 0.8 mm + 0.4)." The authors concluded, "even experienced knee arthroscopy surgeons demonstrate inconsistency in surgical technique when performing microfracture."
7.3. Restoration (Autologous Chondrocyte Implantation)
7.3.1. Carticel (Genzyme Corporation, now Vericel, Inc.)

Articular cartilage cannot repair itself and microfracture, while widespread in adoption, has significant limitations. In an effort to provide a true cartilage repair option, Genzyme Corporation developed the technique of harvesting a biopsy of a patient's own healthy cartilage and amplifying the cells through ex-vivo culture before placing the cells back into the patient and securing them in the defect with a patient-harvested periostal patch to promote integration. Carticel was originally available in 1995 as an unregulated therapy as the cells came from the patient's own body. The FDA was in the process of implementing a new policy for biologics that was released in February 1997 and convened an advisory panel. The panel voted 11-0 with one abstention that Carticel provided a clinical benefit to patient with damage to the articular cartilage of the knee. Carticel recieved accelerated approval from the FDA in August of 1997 after the FDA instituted specific cell therapy guidelines. Under accelerated approval, the FDA required Genzyme to conduct confirmatory post-marketing studies which it completed in 2007, after which it approved new labeling that incorporated the safety and efficacy data from the STAR trial.

There have now been several published reports of long term results following ACI. The surgical procedure was described by Petersen et al. YEAR? showing functional improvement at 2 years and further improvement at long term follow-up between 5 and 11 years following implantation for 44 patients with osteochondritis dissecans or with defects on the femoral condyle alone or with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The modified Cincinnati Knee Score was significantly higher both at 2 years and at long term follow-up when compared to the baseline score. There was an increase in the Knee Score from 2 years and long term follow-up, but the significance of this increase was not discussed. Of note, there were 10 treatment failures (16%) of the 61 patients enrolled. Earlier data from what is believed to be part of the same group of patients was presented by Petersen et al. YEAR? These earlier data showed that the modified Cincinnati Knee Scores were statistically improved at baseline compared with the post-operative scores. These results are consistent with the later findings.19

Henderson et al. YEAR? described two series of consecutive patients treated with ACI who were followed for 12 and 24 months, respectively. There was a reduction in the Objective International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores in both groups at 3 months that essentially returned to baseline by 12 months. There was no statistical difference between the 12 and 24 month scores. The Subjective Knee Score was significantly higher at 12 months than at baseline, and this trend continued at 24 months, but the increase was not significant. Similarly, the ICRS Functional Knee Status was significantly higher at 12 months than at baseline, and even a bit higher at 24 months, but again, the 24 month Functional Knee Status was not significantly different than the 12 month scores.21, . The Subjective Knee Score was significantly higher at 12 months than at baseline, and this trend continued at 24 months, but the increase was not significant. Similarly, the ICRS Functional Knee Status was significantly higher at 12 months than at baseline, and even a bit higher at 24 months, but again, the 24 month Functional Knee Status was not significantly different than the 12 month scores.

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

Knutsen et al. YEAR? described a randomized trial of 80 patients that compared ACI to microfracture. Both groups had significantly higher Lysholm scores and reduced pain at one and two year follow-up when compared to the baseline measurements, but there was no statistical difference between the groups. The improvement in the Short Form-36 Health Survey (SF-36) score in the first two years was significantly higher for the microfracture group. All other results from the two methods yielded similar clinical results.

In a randomized trial comparing ACI to mosaicplasty, Bentley, et al. YEAR? found that the Cincinnati Rating Scores were better for ACI than mosaicplasty, but not statistically significant. The study included an arthroscopic assessment at one year where ICRS repair scores were assigned. Only 60 of the 100 patients (60%) returned for follow-up. There were 82% of the patients in the ACI group that had a repair score of good or excellent. This is significantly higher than the 34% of the patients in the mosaicplasty group, with at least a good repair score.25 The study included an arthroscopic assessment at one year where ICRS repair scores were assigned. Only 60 of the 100 patients (60%) returned for follow-up.

In their 2017 meta-analysis, Schuette, et al. [21], guide their readers through a brief history of the evolution of ACI, a restorative approach to chondral defects. They write:

"ACI is a 2-step procedure in which chondrocytes are first arthroscopically harvested and cultured in vitro. The second procedure involves injecting the chondral defect with the cultured cells and then covering them with a periosteal patch (first-generation ACI) or collagen membrane (second-generation ACI). Issues negatively affecting clinical outcomes, such as periosteal patch hypertrophy associated with the first-generation ACI and extensive suturing and cell leakage associated with second generation ACI, have led to the development of third generation ACI, otherwise known as matrix-assisted autologous chondrocyte transplantation (MACT). In MACT, cultured chondrocytes are seeded into a matrix scaffold and then fixed to the chondral defect with fibrin glue. MACT was first introduced into clinical practice in Europe in 1998. Third-generation ACI was just recently approved by the Food and Drug Administration in the United States [MACI by Vericel, Inc., in December of 2016], with several additional clinical trials currently underway."

With both Carticel and MACI, the body of clinical evidence for autologous chondrocyte implantation was collected in larger defects of approximately 5 cm2, with concomitant procedures and previous microfacture failures, whereas current FDA guidance has required far stricter inclusion/exclusion criteria. Upon approval of MACI by FDA, Vericel, Inc., chose to conclude the commercialization of Carticel in Summer of 2017, and the product is no longer sold to clinicians. The underlying patient biopsies originally used for Carticel were transitioned to MACI upon commercialization in early 2017.

7.3.2. MACI (Vericel, Inc.)

In the MACI technique, in the initial arthroscopic procedure, chondrocytes are harvested from a non-weight-bearing articular surface and cultured ex vivo in a monolayer. These cultured chondrocytes are then seeded on one side of a membrane comprised of Type I and Type III porcine collagen. During the second procedure, performed arthroscopically or via a mini-arthrotomy, the chondrocyte-seeded side of the membrane is placed against the subchondral bone surface and affixed using a fibrin glue [22].

As referenced earlier, MACI received FDA approval for US commercialization in December of 2016. Key clinical evidence for MACI came from the SUMMIT [Demonstrate the Superiority of MACI Implant to Microfracture Treatment] multi-center study, whose results were published by Saris, et al.

Page 19 of 138

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

[23]. The investigators randomized patients with ≥1 focal chondral defect (Outerbridge grade III or IV and defect size ≥3 cm2) on either the femoral condyles or trochlea into either treatment with MACI or microfracture. Only patients with a Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) pain value <55 were enrolled. The co-primary efficacy endpoint was the change in KOOS pain and function subscores from baseline to 2 years. Secondary and tertiary endpoints included: histological evaluation and MRI assessments of structural repair tissue, treatment failure, the remaining 3 KOOS subscales, and safety.

A total of 144 patients were enrolled, 72 in each treatment group; 137 patients (95%) completed the two-year follow-up (70 in the MACI group and 67 in the microfracture group). The mean defect size was equivalent between the two groups (4.9 cm2 for MACI and 4.7 cm2 for microfracture). The mean patient ages were 34.8 (MACI) and 32.9 (microfracture). At the two-year follow-up, the change over baseline in the KOOS pain and function subscores for MACI was significantly higher than the microfracture group (KOOS pain: MACI, 37.0 to 82.5 vs. microfracture, 35.5 to 70.9; KOOS function: MACI, 14.9 to 60.9 vs. microfracture, 12.6 to 48.7; p = 0.001). Significant improvements in the other KOOS subscales were seen in the MACI patients vs. the microfracture patients. Though repair tissue quality was "good" via histology/MRI assessments, no difference was seen between the two treatments. In this study, a "responder" was defined as someone that realized at least a 10-point improvement in both the KOOS pain and function subscales. At 2 years, 87.5% of patients in the MACI group were responders, while 68.1% of the microfracture patients were responders. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) related to the study treatment were similar between the two groups (MACI: 34.7% and microfracture: 38.9%). The most common TEAEs related to the treatment were treatment failure, arthralgia, and joint swelling.
7.3.3. NeoCart (Histogenics, Inc.)

Like MACI, the NeoCart product begins by harvesting healthy chondrocytes from a non-weight-bearing portion of the knee. Unlike MACI, however, these chondrocytes are cultured on a three-dimensional "honeycomb-like" bovine-derived Type I collagen scaffold within a low oxygen-tension custom bioreactor designed to mimic the intra-articular environment [22]. The goal is to create a neocartilaginous implant that possesses increased glycosaminoglycan (GAG) and type-II collagen production. Thus, instead of implanting cells with the potential to differentiate and form hyaline cartilage, NeoCart "is a matured tissue-like implant containing hyaline GAGs designed to provide a more rapid and potentially sustained therapeutic effect for articular cartilage repair" [24]. The NeoCart implant is secured to the subchondral bone using a proprietary resorbable tissue adhesive (CT3, Histogenics, Waltham, MA).
7.3.3.1. Phase 1 Study:

The Phase I multi-center study was conducted in 2005 to assess the safety of NeoCart. It was an open label, single arm study of 8 patients with a single focal cartilage defect of the knee who were followed for five (5) years post implantation. The average age was 38 years, 63% were male. Baseline mean IKDC was 57±25 and 75% had undergone previous knee surgery. There were only two related safety events with dislodgement of the NeoCart implant at 1 month and failure of the NeoCart implant to remain in place during the operative procedure. While the focus of the study was safety, efficacy data was also gathered.

Page 20 of 138

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

Throughout the 5-years post-implant, study subjects demonstrated improved ROM, function and pain scores. Average ROM was 128±10 at baseline and increased at 6-months post-procedure (131±8) and continued to improve throughout the study time course (5 years 137±5). IKDC function scores also increased throughout the study, peaking at 36-months post-procedure at 78+21. This increase was greater than 20 points over the average baseline value (57±25). IKDC decreased slightly at 4 and 5 years but remained improved over baseline values. One subject, 03-004, presented improved IKDC results only at 2 and 3 years, and returned to levels below baseline at 4 and 5 years. Average baseline VAS scores were 33 and decreased (improved) throughout the study, with an average decrease of 20 points from year 1 through year 5. With respect to MRI, 88% of subjects demonstrated good fill at the defect site and evidence of T2 stratification at 1 year.
7.3.3.2. Phase 2 Study

The Phase II NeoCart study was a prospective multi-center study conducted between 2006 and 2008 that compared the performance and safety profile of NeoCart versus microfracture in a controlled, randomized (2:1), multi-center clinical study. The objective of the study was to further evaluate the safety of NeoCart to fill articular cartilage defects in the knee, gather additional efficacy data, identify clinically meaningful endpoints, identify appropriate patient populations, and to obtain additional data to be used in the design of future clinical studies A total of thirty-five patients were enrolled at 7 sites in the United States. Five patients were excluded during arthroscopy, leaving 30 patients, 21 in the NeoCart cohort and 9 in the microfracture cohort. The rehabilitation protocol, originally developed for microfracture recovery, was identical for both arms. Performance measurements included the following self-reported patient surveys: The International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) form (subjective); Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) pain, symptoms, activities of daily living (ADL), quality of life (QOL), and sports scales; Short Form-36 (SF-36) questionnaire; and a visual analog scale (VAS) pain scale. Clinical assessment and questionnaires were conducted at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-procedure. In addition, the researchers conducted a "responder analysis" by defining a "responder" as a patient that demonstrated a change in their KOOS pain score of ≥12 points and a change in the IKDC function score of ≥20 points.

Of the 30 treated patients, the patients were primarily male (90.5% in the NeoCart group and 66.7% in the microfracture group), white race (81.0% in the NeoCart group and 88.9% in the microfracture group) and had a mean age at baseline of 41.39 years in the NeoCart group and 38.84 in the microfracture group. The mean BMI was statistically significantly higher in the NeoCart group with a BMI of 28.88 kg/m2 compared to 25.37 kg/m2 in the microfracture group (p=0.0096; see The location of injury for the majority of patients was the medial condyle (71.4% of patients in the NeoCart group and 66.7% in the microfracture group). The mean age of injury in the treated knee was similar in both groups (2.80 years in the NeoCart group and 2.22 years in the microfracture group). Mean lesion sizes prior to treatment and with treatment were also clinically similar between the treatment groups. A greater percentage of patients in the NeoCart group (71.4%) had a prior surgical history to the study knee compared to 44.4% of patients in the microfracture group. All other demographics and baseline characteristics were generally clinically balanced between the treatment groups

The safety analysis for the phase II study was favorable with no concerning issues. No clinically meaningful differences were noted in AE rates between the NeoCart and microfracture treatment groups. The most common TEAE assessed as related to NeoCart was Arthralgia; this was also the most common

Page 21 of 138

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

procedure-related TEAE in the microfracture group. There were no SAEs assessed as related to NeoCart. One death occurred in the microfracture group completely unrelated to the treatment and occurring at the very end of the 5-year study period.

There were no statistically significant differences in the mean change from baseline in range of motion between the NeoCart and microfracture groups at any time point. Within treatment groups, there was a statistically significant increase in the mean range of motion change from baseline in the NeoCart group at 12 months in both the passive (4.2; p=0.0301) and active (5.4; p=0.0105) parameters. Similarly, at the 5-year visit, the NeoCart group had statistically significant increases in the range of motion change from baseline in both the passive (12.1 degrees; p=0.0003) and active (11.9 degrees; p=0.0010) parameters. In the microfracture group, there were no statistically significant changes from baseline in the IKDC mean range of motion at 12 months and 5 years.

For IKDC subjective score changes there were statistically significant differences in the mean changes from baseline for subjective scores between the NeoCart and microfracture groups at the 1 year (14.90, p=0.0090) and 2 year (13.15, p=0.0428) time points; At 12 months, the NeoCart group had a mean IKDC subjective score increase from baseline of 31.25 (p <0.0001) which increased to 34.10 (p<0.0001) by the 5 year time point. The microfracture group also had improvements in the mean IKDC subjective scores. At 12 months, the microfracture group had a mean IKDC subjective score increase from baseline of 16.35 (p=0.0002), which increased to 37.07 (p=0.0149) by the 5 year time point. The KOOS instrument assessed the following 5 subscales: symptoms/stiffness, pain, daily living function, sports and recreational activities function, and quality of life. In general, there were statistically significant improvements from baseline seen in each of the subscales at the majority of time points in the NeoCart group. There were a few statistically significant increases from baseline at the protocol required time points noted in the KOOS subscale scores in the microfracture group. Overall, the increases from baseline in the KOOS scores were greater in the NeoCart group, with some statistically significant differences in mean change from baseline between the groups. The pain subscale indicates highly statistically significant improvements from baseline at each time point in the NeoCart group, as well as statistically significant differences in mean change from baseline between groups at 6 months, 12 months, 3 years, and 4 years.

A dual threshold responder analysis was an exploratory efficacy endpoint with the definition of a responder being a KOOS pain score improvement of 12 points and IKDC improvement of 20 points. At 12 months 66.7% of the NeoCart patients were responders and only 22.2% of the microfracture patients were P=0.0457).

The NeoCart group had statistically significant improvements from baseline on the SF-36 in the mean physical component summary scores at all protocol-specified time points. The microfracture group had statistically significant increases from baseline on the SF-36 in the mean physical component summary scores at years 1 to 5. In the mental component summary of the SF-36, the only statistically significant increase from baseline was in the microfracture group at the 3-month time point. No differences between groups in the SF-36 mean physical and mental summary scores reached statistical significance

Statistically significant mean improvements from baseline in the VAS pain assessment were seen in each of the three categories (lowest, average, and highest pain) at each time point in the NeoCart group. No statistically significant mean increases from baseline were seen in the VAS pain assessment in any of the categories (lowest, average, and highest pain) at any of the protocol-specified time points in the microfracture group. There were also several statistically significant differences noted between the

groups in the VAS pain assessment categories (lowest, average, and highest pain), with greater decreases in pain seen in the NeoCart group
7.4. The role of Physical Therapy/Rehabilitiation

All patients undergoing treatment for cartilage damage of the knee irrespective of treatment modality should undergo a monitored rehabilitation program to ensure optimum results. In the article, "Functional Outcomes after Surgical Management of Articular Cartilage Lesions in the Knee: A Systematic Literature Review to Guide Postoperative Rehabilitation," Schmitt, et al. [16] conclude from their research, "Significant quadriceps femoris strength deficits, gait deviations, and functional deficits persist for 5 to 7 years following ACI and microfracture surgical procedures. Future research regarding rehabilitation interventions to help mitigate these deficits is warranted." As detailed in articles by Wilk, et al. [17] and Mithoefer, et al. [18], optimal post-operative rehabilitation of the knee after articular cartilage repair should be individualized to the patient: tailored to the patient's age and BMI, his/her defect size, depth, and location, the repair technique used, duration of symptoms prior to intervention, and evolving quality of the cartilage [18]. As both sets of researchers instruct, the phases of post- operative physical therapy should mirror the biologic phase of wound repair: during Phase 1 (proliferative phase) of cartilage repair, the initial healing benefits from a reduction in swelling and a gradual restoration of passive range of motion and weightbearing [17]. During Phase 2 (transition phase), a patient proceeds from gradual to full weightbearing with a focus on joint function restoration. During the final phase (remodeling/maturation), the goal is to have the patient return to full activity. Recognize the inherent variability associated with post-operative rehabilitation: failure to individualize treatment to the patient's condition, and failure to match the strength and motion restoration to the evolving healing of the cartilage defect, can all lead to considerable variability in patient outcomes.

Ebert, et al., [19] demonstrated that differences in rehabilitation regimens could alter the outcomes after chondral injury restoration using matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation (MACI, discussed below).above) An accelerated weightbearing regimen (full weightbearing at 8 weeks post-procedure) was compared to a traditional regimen (full weightbearing at 11 weeks post-procedure) by measuring pain and various functional metrics at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-surgery. Patients in the accelerated weightbearing regimen reported significantly lower pain and demonstrated improved 6- minute walk distances compared to the those in the traditional rehabilitation regimen. While it is imperative to highlight that these patients received chondral restoration rather than microfracture - and recognizing that the needs of graft repair healing may be different -research by Ebert, et al., is meant to emphasize that differences in rehabilitation can affect surgical outcomes in treating chondral defects.

That said, research by Marder et al. [20], suggested that the impact of rehabilitation on functional outcomes can be secondary to other, more significant factors. In their study, patients with focal full- thickness chondral defects less than 2 cm2 treated with microfracture entered one of two rehabilation groups post-surgery: in one group, patients were treated with non-weight bearing and continuous passive motion (CPM) for six weeks, while in the second group, patients were allowed weight bearing as tolerated and did not use CPM. Outcomes were assessed using the Lysholm knee rating scale augmented by the Tegner method of activity evaluation. No significant difference was detected between the two groups when comparing the pre-operative and post-operative Lysholm scores. It is possible that the healing of small focal defects after microfracture is insensitive to differences in post-surgical rehabilitation.

8. STUDY OBJECTIVES

The objectives of this study are 1) to evaluate the safety and efficacy of, NeoCart, in the repair of cartilage defects of the femoral condyles and/or trochlea and 2) to compare NeoCart safety and efficacy to microfracture treatment.

blocks.text:
This was a prospective, controlled, randomized, multi-center clinical study. The initial planned sample size of 245 was randomized 2:1 between NeoCart and microfracture at up to 40 investigational sites. Randomization was done at arthroscopy, at which time final patient eligibility was determined. Neither surgeon nor patient was blinded to treatment. The International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) Objective knee examination and the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reads were blinded.

The primary analysis of success is a responder analysis at 12 months in which the proportion of responders in the treatment arm is compared to the proportion of responders in the control arm. In this study, a responder is defined as a patient with an increase of at least 12 points on the KOOS pain assessment and at least 20 points on the IKDC Subjective assessment at the 12-month visit. The data was tested for superiority.

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

was submitted to the IND under a Special Protocol Assessment request and was approved by FDA on March 10, 2009.The trial was required to be a prospective, multi-center randomized trial of superiority comparing the success of NeoCart to that of microfracture. The primary endpoint was agreed upon to be one year with continuation through years 2 and 3. Although the trial was designed prior to the guidance document it complied with the requirement to demonstrate superiority and to have two different validated scores for pain and function endpoints to assess for meaningful improvement. The agreed upon endpoints were KOOS pain and IKDC subjective function scores which are very well accepted validated scoring systems for both pain and function of knee pathology. All KOOS and IKDC subscores were prospectively obtained at baseline and at all post-procedure visits

We did that, and describe the prospective collection of KOOS and IKDC as starting point, per the now available guidance.

The guidance document does not require that these two different tests be combined into a dual threshold primary responder analysis which was done in the NeoCart trial. This addeds an additional hurdle as a patient was required to reach the success levels for both measures to be considered a positive responder.

To meet the objectives the primary endpoint for the Phase III study was defined as a test of superiority (one-sided Pearson's chi-square test, a=0.025) vs microfracture, in terms of a composite clinical success (CCS) used in a dual threshold responder analysis for pain and function at 12-months post index surgery. A subject was considered a responder if they achieved both of the following outcomes:

· An improvement of at least 12 points in outcome compared to baseline on the KOOS pain assessment test, and

· An improvement of at least 20 points in outcome compared to baseline on the IKDC subjective test.

These improvement thresholds were set based upon the available data at the time and above what are currently considered minimum clinically important differences (MCID) for improvements on pain and function as established in the literature. The MCID had not been well established at the time of the writing of the protocol and the thresholds were determined with considerable input from the performance in the Phase II study where microfracture performed poorly.

The current standards for clinically meaningful IKDC scores start at a 6-point improvement as early as 6 months and increase to 15 or 16 points at later timeframes. For KOOS pain, the meaningful clinically important difference is seen in the 8 to 10-point range. Both thresholds in the NeoCart trial (KOOS of 12 points and IKDC of 20 points) were higher than what was and is now seen as a minimum clinically meaningful or important difference, or MCID (Collins, 2011).

Microfracture was used as the concurrent control for the NeoCart Phase III study as it is the most common surgical treatment modality, and current standard of care both at the time of the study design and persistent today despite the limitations of the procedure as noted for both efficacy and durability. Microfracture continues to be used as both active and as an historical control in other ongoing studies for treatment of knee cartilage defects based upon FDA guidance. Despite extensive use of microfracture commercially over the last two decades in broad patient populations, a treatment effect in the population evaluated in this Phase III study is not well established due to a paucity of adequate and well-controlled studies that are designed in accordance to the now available FDA guidance. The sponsor established inclusion and exclusion criteria and a study population based on FDA and clinical expert feedback to provide the microfracture treatment the best possible chance to succeed and attempt to institute clinical equipoise for the study, as there are well-known limitations to this treatment. Key inclusion and exclusion criteria were lesions less than 6cm2, BMI less than 35, no concomitant knee surgical procedures, and no prior microfracture treatments allowed.

The FDA published the guidance "Preparation of IDEs and INDs for Products Intended to Repair or Replace Knee Cartilage" ("FDA Guidance") for products indicated for treatment of knee cartilage in December 2011. Although the NeoCart Phase III study was initiated prior to the FDA guidance, the study design is consistent with the FDA guidance, including the requirement for improvement in both pain and function and a test of superiority versus an active concurrent control (i.e. microfracture). It includes an extension phase of an additional 3-years (assessment at 2-year and 3-year timepoints post- surgery) to evaluate durability. blocks.text: 9.3. Selection of Study Population
Patients were considered for enrollment into the study if they met all of the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria prior to randomization.
9.3.1. Inclusion Criteria
9.3.1.1. General Inclusion Criteria

Patients meeting all of the following criteria may have been included into study. The patient must have been:

· Able and willing to give informed consent.

· 18 years to 59 years of age. (increased from original age limit of 55 Rev 8 November 10, 2015).

· Symptomatic with knee pain indicative of an articular cartilage injury of the distal femur. Baseline KOOS pain score must be ≤80 and baseline IKDC Subjective score must be ≤70.

· Medically able to undergo arthroscopy, arthrotomy for NeoCart implantation, and serial MRIs.

· Females must be post-menopausal or practicing an acceptable form of birth control.

· The following prior procedures are permitted after ≥ 3 months have passed since the procedure if, at the discretion of the investigator, pain is determined to be specifically referable to the cartilage defect and not residual from the prior injury or surgical procedure:

o Partial meniscectomy (<50% radial width, preserving fully intact peripheral rim) on the study knee

o Meniscal repair on the study knee

o Ligament reconstruction on either knee
9.3.1.2. Arthroscopic Inclusion Criteria

Patients meeting all of the following criteria may have been included into study:

· At least one ICRS grade 3 or 4A lesion located on the femur (lateral/medial condyles and/or trochlea that would be treatable by microfracture. ICRS grade 4A lesions must have no substantive bone loss. Trochlear lesions must not be associated with clinically significant patellar malalignment.

Page 26 of 138
CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

· One or two non-contiguous and non-opposing lesions may be treated as long as each lesion meets the arthroscopic inclusion and exclusion criteria and the total surface area of both treated lesions is ≤ 6 cm2 (size of NeoCart). With respect to the individual lesion size, each treated lesion must be at least 1 cm in one linear dimension. The range of lesion sizes treated shall be between 0.5 cm2- 6 cm2.

· Permitted concomitant procedures include:

o Medial or lateral partial meniscectomy of less than 50% radial width, preserving a fully intact peripheral rim.

o Removal of loose bodies or impending loose bodies.

o Debridement/chondroplasty of non-study lesions.

o Synovectomy.

o Judicious excision of tissue from the study lesion(s) to the extent necessary to facilitate measurement and grading of the lesion(s) in order to complete the final qualification step prior to randomization.
9.3.2. Exclusion Criteria
9.3.2.1. Pre-Procedure Exclusion Criteria

Any patient who met any of the following criteria was not included into this study.

· Any previous surgical treatment of the study defect (such as abrasion arthroplasty, abrasion chondroplasty, multiple drilling or microfracture). Prior debridement or shaving of the articular cartilage/chondroplasty of the study lesion was permitted but must have been performed >3 months prior to the study arthroscopy.

· The following prior procedures within 3 months prior to study arthroscopy, in the judgment of the investigator, if pain was not specifically referable to the cartilage defect:

o Partial meniscectomy or meniscal repair on the study knee

o Ligament reconstruction on either knee

· Surgery on the contralateral knee within 3 months prior to study arthroscopy.

· Body Mass Index (BMI) > 35 kg/m2.

· Radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis, Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 3 or greater.

· Malalignment greater than 3 degrees outside the mechanical axis from the contralateral knee, or malalignment requiring surgical correction.

· Symptomatic pathology of the contralateral knee.

· Any form of inflammatory arthritis.

· Ankylosing spondylitis.

· Synovioma, hemangioma, pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS), or other neoplasms in the knee.

· Any condition requiring chemotherapy.

· Positive pregnancy test or intention to become pregnant during the year following treatment.

· Known history of allergy to bovine products or gentamycin.

· Any autoimmune disease.

· Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), chronic hepatitis B or C viral infection.

· Insulin-dependent diabetes.

· Clinically significant or symptomatic vascular or neurologic disorder of the lower extremities.

· Current drug or alcohol abuse.

· Evidence suggesting inability to comply with the Protocol.

· Smoking habit of more than 1 pack of cigarettes per week and/or were frequent users (>1/week) of chewing tobacco. The number of smokers were limited to 10% of the enrolled patients.

· Any concomitant painful or disabling disease of the hips or lower limbs that would have interfered with the evaluation of the afflicted knee.

· Treatment with specific osteoarthritis drugs, such as chondroitin sulfate, diacerein, n- glucosamine, piascledine, and capsaicin, within the last 2 weeks.

· Corticosteroid therapy by systemic or intra-articular route within the last month of baseline or intramuscular or oral corticosteroids within the last 2 weeks.

· Intra-articular injections of hyaluronic acid into the afflicted knee within the last 6 months.

· Status as a participant in an investigational research trial within the last 3 months.
9.3.2.2. Arthroscopic Exclusion Criteria

Any patient who met any of the following criteria was not included into this study:

· Subchondral bone loss.

· Untreated ACL and/or posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) deficiency or ligamentous instability in the index knee.

· Study lesion requiring a concomitant procedure intended as a therapeutic intervention to the study lesion, e.g., debridement/chondroplasty, or that may have altered the mechanics of the joint, e.g., osteotomy. Permitted concomitant procedures are detailed in the inclusion criteria above.

· Meniscus whose rim was less than 50% normal radial width or whose peripheral rim was not fully intact.

· ICRS Grade 3 or 4 kissing lesions.

· ICRS Grade 3B or greater patellar or tibial lesions associated with pain specifically and reproducibly referable to the untreated lesions(s).

Patients were assigned to treatment based upon a 2:1 randomization scheme. Randomization took place at the time of arthroscopy. Individual blinded patient randomization envelopes were created based upon this schedule design and distributed to the investigational sites. For each patient, site personnel would open the envelope during the arthroscopic procedure to determine the treatment assignment. Envelopes were to be opened sequentially within a strata and were created by Biostatistical Consulting Inc.

The Randomization List used to create envelopes was created using two strata (Stratum 1 (BMI < 28kg/m2) and Stratum 2 (BMI ≥ 28kg/m2). Stratum one was placed in blue envelopes and stratum two in black envelopes. Randomization was created by site and stratum using block sizes of six. The randomization scheme and codes are provided in Section 16.1.7.

Both the NeoCart and microfracture procedures were performed by the same study investigators. Rehabilitation status was assessed at each visit. 9.5.2. Arthroscopy Procedure

The arthroscopy procedures were scheduled in order to allow ample time for lab processing, MRI image submission and core lab baseline letter return prior to the procedure. All required baseline results were available before the time of arthroscopy. Data was recorded during the procedure to document that the patient met the selection criteria. Data collection included assessments of all cartilage defects and status of all structures in the knee compartments.
9.5.3. Biopsy Procedure
The steps for the Biopsy Procedure were performed in accordance with the Instructions for Use (IFU), after patient randomization to the NeoCart cohort.
9.5.4. Microfracture Procedure

The following steps, described in more detail by Steadman, et al. [27], were performed after patient randomization to the microfracture cohort:

a. Debride the lesion of all remaining unstable cartilage. All loose or marginally attached cartilage from the surrounding rim is to be debrided to form a stable, perpendicular edge of healthy, viable cartilage.

b. A curette is used to carefully remove the calcified layer from the base of the lesion. The calcified cartilage comprises a layer between the deep zone of cartilage and the subchondral bone and this layer can increase in thickness with age. The calcified layer can be difficult to differentiate visually but can be distinguished more easily from the hard, underlying

Page 31 of 138

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

subchondral bone plate by tactile feedback. The use of a curette provides better manual feedback than an arthroscopic shaver and reduces the risk of excessive debridement.

c. Make multiple holes in the exposed subchondral bone plate using an arthroscopic awl. A Linvatec Corp. awl is recommended. The holes should be made perpendicular to the surface.

d. Microfracture holes should initially be made around the periphery immediately adjacent to the healthy stable cartilage, and then progressing toward the center of the lesion. The holes should be made 3-4 mm apart and should be to a depth of 2 to 4 mm. A minimum spacing should be maintained so that one hole does not break into another and damage the subchondral plate between holes. There should be visible marrow fat droplets and blood released from the microfracture holes.

e. Evacuate all fluid and close the access sites without placement of intra-articular drains and dress the incision following standard hospital procedures.

f. Post-surgical recovery care was conducted in accordance with standard hospital procedures and the patient is to be discharged at the discretion of the investigator.
9.5.5. NeoCart Implant Procedure

The NeoCart derived from the biopsy sample was intended to be implanted into the same patient. Therefore, utmost care was taken to match the identity of the patient to the patient indicated on the NeoCart label. An arthrotomy procedure was required for NeoCart implantation into the defect bed. The following steps were followed during the implant procedure:

1. The patient was prepared for arthrotomy using conventional preparation. Standard hospital procedures were followed to gain access to the defect.

2. Any fragments and debris from the defect were removed and the defect bed was

smoothed. The zone of calcified cartilage was carefully scraped away taking care not to penetrate the subchondral bone. A tourniquet was not used during the procedure so that inadvertent bleeding from the subchondral bone could be ascertained and stopped prior to the implantation of the NeoCart.

3. The NeoCart was removed from the shipping container. The size and shape of the defect to be treated were determined and the NeoCart was trimmed to provide an implant piece that fit the defect dimensions. The trimmed NeoCart was then positioned into the defect to confirm the NeoCart fit.

4. A CT3 resorbable tissue adhesive kit was then opened and prepared. The CT3 was used within 20 minutes, or the material was discarded and new CT3 mixed.

5. A small amount of CT3 was evenly spread into the defect bed, and then the trimmed NeoCart implant was placed.

6. After NeoCart placement, moderate pressure was briefly applied to the implant to allow the CT3 to set. The NeoCart implant was then affixed to the defect. (The NeoCart implant was not to be repositioned after initial placement.)

7. A thin layer of CT3 was spread over the NeoCart and also extended the CT3 layer onto the native articular cartilage surface. The CT3 was to extend at least 2 mm past the NeoCart around the periphery of the defect. The surface of the CT3 was also to be as smooth as possible, without being proud in relation to the surrounding articular cartilage.

8. The Curing Component buffer was applied to the CT3 and the CT3 was allowed time to set. The setting time was accelerated by the use of the buffer. Any excess CT3 was trimmed to create a smooth surface.

9. Following the surface application of CT3, the leg was carefully extended to avoid excessive shear stresses on the NeoCart. No range of motion evaluations were performed, and additional flexing of the knee was to be avoided.

Page 32 of 138

CLINICAL STUDY REPORT

10. The arthrotomy was closed and the incision dressed following standard hospital procedures. A brace was applied to immobilize the knee and locked at an angle appropriate to minimize joint movement at the Investigator's discretion, depending on the implant location. The patient was then fitted with anti-embolism stockings to minimize the risk of embolism.

11. Post-surgical recovery care was conducted in accordance with standard hospital procedures and the patient was discharged at the discretion of the Investigator
Rehabilitation

Rehabilitation was guided by the investigator in general phases described below and advanced according to each patient's specific issues (healing and function). The primary driver of the very proscriptive rehabilitation protocol was the microfracture procedure and the seminal work by Dr. Steadman regarding how to optimize success of microfracture. This rehabilitation plan was individualized, phased and included a detailed description of activities and limitations. It that incorporated specific strengthening and conditioning goals to be attained prior to advancing to the next phase of rehabilitation and to facilitate successful recovery from surgery, keeping in mind the patient's goals and previous activity level. Exercises were specified, and patients trained to complete the exercises, but the specific exercises and training on how to perform the exercises was done at the discretion of the investigator. Patients were contacted periodically for reinforcement and support in the performance of the exercises.
Use of Knee Brace:

Patients with condylar lesions in either study arm were not required to wear a knee brace but may have been prescribed a brace at the investigator's discretion. Patients with trochlear lesions should have been placed in a locking brace immediately and for at least 6 weeks post-operatively, with the unlocking schedule determined by the investigator. If the investigator prescribed a knee brace for patients, this was documented in the patient's file.
Prophylaxis for Thromboembolic Disease (TED):

For any patient placed into a knee immobilizer or partially- or fully-locked knee brace following any study procedure, two methods of thromboembolic disease (TED) prophylaxis, aspirin and a thigh-high or knee-high compression stocking for the operative extremity, was ordered for the duration of immobilization/bracing. The dosage of aspirin and the period of daily use of compression stockings was determined by the investigator.
Continuous passive motion therapy (CPM):

Continuous passive motion therapy (CPM) began on the day of the procedure for all patients not placed into a knee immobilizer or hinged knee brace with restricted motion. For patients placed into a knee brace or immobilizer, and at the discretion of the investigator, CPM began as early as the day of the procedure but, in any case, no later than the first post-operative visit. CPM continued for a minimum of 6 weeks and a maximum of 8 weeks. All patients were recommended to perform CPM for 6-10 hours per day, but investigators could alter the daily amount based on each patient's needs.
Weightbearing Status:

NeoCart patients with small condylar lesions that were less than 2cm2 with a circumferentially stable margin of intact cartilage were limited to toe touch weightbearing until the first post-operative visit (10 days) and increased weightbearing as tolerated after that visit.

NeoCart patients with condylar lesions that were greater than or equal to 2 cm2 or with lesions that do not have a circumferentially stable margin of intact cartilage were limited to toe-touch weightbearing for 4-6 weeks after implant and then increased weightbearing as tolerated.

Both NeoCart and microfracture patients with trochlear lesions were allowed weightbearing as tolerated with a brace. 9.5.7. Efficacy Parameters

The primary efficacy study endpoint was defined as a test of superiority (one-sided Pearson's Chi- square₮ test, a=0.025) vs microfracture, in terms of a composite clinical success (CCS) used in a dual- threshold responder analysis based on improvement in knee-specific pain and function at 1 year using the IKDC Subjective knee exam and the Pain domain score from the KOOS Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score.

Patients were required to demonstrate both an improvement in KOOS pain of ≥ 12 points and IKDC subjective score of ≥ 20 points to be a positive responder.

The IKDC instrument is a validated region-specific patient-oriented outcome measure of symptoms, function, and sports activity. A score of 100 represents no limitation with activities of daily living or sports activities and absence of symptoms. The normative score for this age group is about 90.
The KOOS has five separate scores:

blocks.text:
Pain, Symptoms, Activities of Daily Living (ADL), Sport/Recreation, and Quality of Life (QoL). Similar to IKDC, a KOOS Pain score of 100 represents no pain. The KOOS Pain assessment is preferred over a VAS Pain scale (to be evaluated in supporting analyses) because it evaluates pain levels using a pain frequency scale (never, rarely, sometimes, often, always) in relation to specific knee activities of daily living (e.g. walking, climbing, sitting, pivoting, etc.).

The dual threshold is a composite score inclusive of the IKDC subjective and KOOS pain values. By The two sub-scores were used as the primary endpoint whiledefinition this means that all individual IKDC and KOOS endpoints were prospectively collected both as exploratory analyses and for purposes of conducting the dual-threshold responder analysis.

The secondary efficacy endpoints included time to full weight-bearing, 'Treatment failure' (defined as >8-point deterioration in KOOS Pain score at 1 year compared to baseline) and the presence of mature collagen layering as assessed by MRI T2 mapping at 1 year.

9.6. Data Quality Assurance

Data required according to the protocol were recorded in the web-based eCRFs-EDC (electronic data capture system) on iMedNet platform created and managed by Health Policy Associates. On 1/8/16, the data was migrated to this system as the study EDC was originally hosted by ProSoft. All data were imported into iMedNet and SDV status and signatures were applied in accordance with how the records were entered into Prosoft at the time of transfer.

Auto queries were generated in the EDC system for data that did not meet specifications or when required fields were skipped. Inconsistencies in the data were queried to the investigators via the electronic data capture system; answers to queries or changes to the data were made by an authorized member of the investigator's staff. Changes are documented via the Audit Trail File (ATF).

Manual queries (to be answered by site staff) were raised during source data verification, medical or safety review and data management review. Additionally, to monitor and data manager manual queries, HPA programed edit checks to look for various inconsistencies based on review of exports or team feedback. Plausibility checks were performed to ensure correctness and completeness of the data. Some examples include missing forms, missing fields, unexpected values, or inconsistency across forms. The result of running these checks is a list of known issues, which HPA reviewed and worked with clinical and data teams to resolve. In addition to monitor and data manager manual queries, HPA programed edit checks to look for various inconsistencies based on review of exports or team feedback. Some examples include missing forms, missing fields, unexpected values, or inconsistency across forms. The result of running these checks is a list of known issues, which HPA reviewed and worked with clinical and data teams to resolve. Once the sites respond to raised queries in the database, the queries were reviewed and closed as appropriate.

Laboratory and antibody data were received per the protocol schedule and abnormal values were entered electronically and merged to the eCRF data (but not uploaded into the EDC system).

The sponsor's data management function was responsible for data processing, in accordance with the sponsor's data management procedures.

After all data through the 1 year primary endpoint were entered and all queries were resolved, the database was closed on August 23rd, 2018. Unblinding took place on August 28th, 2018.

9.7.5.4. Test for site heterogeneity in treatment effect

blocks.text: For the ITT analysis, a standard Breslow-Day test of homogeneity of the odds ratios across sites was performed. Sites with less than five patients were combined into a single pooled site. If the Breslow-Day p-value was less than 0.05 and if there were a number of sites enrolling a relatively small number of patients, site were assessed as a random effect. Specifically, SAS Proc GLMMIX was to be used to construct a test for superiority accounting for random site effects reflecting site-to-site variation in treatment group response rate differences.

blocks.text: 9.7.5.6. Analysis of MRI Data
container_path: 9.7. Statistical Methods Planned in the Protocol and Determination of Sample Size

blocks.text:
All MRI images collected under this protocol were submitted to the MRI Core Lab. The MRI Core Lab was blinded to the randomization arm. Analysis included standard MRI review to assess the quantity of the defect repair during the course of the trial. These MRI findings are divided into anatomic assessments that were made using generally accepted, well-established MRI sequences, and more advanced sequences that allow for the direct, qualitative assessment of the area of defect repair. Standard MRI sequences provide high contrast between fat suppressed bone and cartilage; however, they are not fluid sensitive and are degraded in the postoperative setting due to susceptibility artifact. Fast spin echo sequences with high in-plane resolution provide good cartilage to fluid contrast, making them more sensitive to partial thickness lesions.

In addition to standard MRI review, an advanced T2 MRI image acquisition sequence was used at qualified MRI centers. T2 mapping permits direct, qualitative and quantitative assessment of the collagen component of the extracellular matrix of the NeoCart implant and adjacent articular cartilage. T2 relaxation time is a reproducible MRI parameter that reflects the internuclear reaction, or dephasing, that occurs as a result of transverse relaxation of the excited hydrogen dipoles. The stratification of the T2 signal is indicative of a normal arrangement of the type II collagen fibers within the cartilage repair.

9.7.6. 6. Handling of Dropouts or Missing Data

blocks.text:
Multiple imputation was specified to be used in sensitivity analyses to determine Month 12 responder status when Month 12 CCS was missing. In this approach, "Prediction is based on the patient level of success and failure-not on the two components of success separately."

However, statistical efficiencies can be obtained by using linear regression based multiple imputation [29-32] on the underlying continuous variables of change in KOOS and change IKDC subjective scores separately, rather than on an endpoint defined by collapsing multiple underlying continuous variables. Therefore, missing Month 12 KOOS and IKDC were individually imputed as continuous variables in parallel imputations and then combined to form the CCS. This approach takes advantage of potentially stronger associations among continuous variables. Also, multiple imputation of the individual scores is closer to the LOCF approach specified for the primary analysis. In the primary analysis, LOCF was applied to KOOS pain and IKDC subjective score individually, and then each score is to be dichotomized in order to form the composite clinical endpoint.

The original plan included varying certain model parameters to reflect extremes concerning the impact of missing values on group differences. This type of analysis was retained but was accomplished using conventional tipping point analyses.

blocks.text: 9.7.6.1. Responder analysis
container_path: 9.7. Statistical Methods Planned in the Protocol and Determination of Sample Size
9.7.6. 6. Handling of Dropouts or Missing Data

blocks.text:
When computing responder status in primary analyses, e.g., 1-year composite clinical success in the intent-to-treat (ITT) (as well as in the As-Treated (AT) analyses), the last-observation carried-forward (LOCF) method were used to impute the components of missing KOOS and IKDC. That is, subjects missing 1-year values had their 1 year values replaced by their Month 6 values, if Month 6 was available. If Month 6 is not available, then the Month 3 values were used. If there are no values past baseline, the subject was considered a Month 12 nonresponder in primary efficacy analyses in the ITT analysis set.

Sensitivity analyses based on multiple imputation and on 'tipping point' analyses will also be performed.

Supporting analyses involving group comparisons in mean changes will involve the use of mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) which allows inclusion of all available data including intermediate values of KOOS Pain and IKDC Subjective score changes as well as relevant baseline covariates to inform the contrast of interest.

Covariates will include age, gender, total lesion size at arthroscopy, total lesion size at treatment, BMI, number of study lesions, injury type, most severe lesion ICRS grade, and smoking status. Last- observation-carried-forward imputation will also be conducted for the specified secondary efficacy endpoints. If a patient has no results post-baseline for T2 mapping, they were excluded from analysis. For all other endpoints and outcomes, there was no imputation of missing data with the exception of analysis done on the questionnaires added in version 7 of the protocol and the new exploratory analyses for KOOS Pain and Function at 1 and 2 years.

No data imputation is necessary for time to full weight-bearing because this endpoint was analyzed using survival analysis methods and subjects who terminate the study early were censored as of the time of their last observation. blocks.text: Multiple imputation was used as an alternative to LOCF for imputing missing 1-year responder status in sensitivity analyses for the primary efficacy endpoint. Section 8 provides details concerning the methods to be used. Three questionnaires were added to the study with the approval of version 7 of the protocol (December 12, 2014). Due to the timing of the addition of these questionnaires, patients enrolled under earlier versions of the protocol are missing these questionnaires at baseline and any other visits attended prior to version 7. For this questionnaire data, missing values were imputed up to 1-year using regression based on available timepoints through PROC MI. Multiply imputed inferences from the unadjusted mean differences and the MMRM mean differences were pooled together using PROC MIANALYZE in order to create combined results for each. As more patients were enrolled under versions 7 and 8 of the protocol and fewer patients enrolled under those versions have reached 2-3-year visit windows at the time of submission, extended follow-up visit responses will not be analyzed for Marx activity rating, EQ-5D-5L, or WPAI.

blocks.text: 9.7.7. Interim Analyses
container_path: 9.7. Statistical Methods Planned in the Protocol and Determination of Sample Size

blocks.text:
The original study design included a formal interim analysis to be conducted based on 80-90% of the originally planned sample for the purpose of sample size re-estimation. There was no provision for early stopping for superiority. The interim analysis for sample size re-estimation was not performed as the rate of lost to follow-up (the only nuisance parameter) was lower than anticipated (2.4% by Jan 2017 rather than 7%), and the sponsor decided not to conduct the interim analysis for sample size re- estimation.

Additionally, the original study design included a pre-planned administrative analysis to be conducted "for the sponsor's financial planning purposes with results potentially provided to a small number of individuals responsible for company financing". This was specified to occur when "~75% of patients have been enrolled". No specific statistical analysis was specified for this 'administrative analysis'.

The rigor of this planned "administrative analysis" had been enhanced by pre-planning of a futility analysis based on the determination of conditional power. To this end, a futility analysis was planned take place after 50% of the initially planned sample size (i.e., 123 patients) was due for their month 12 follow-up visit.

However, the iSAP stipulated that the futility analysis "may not be conducted if enrollment is completed or nearly completed by the time that 50% of patients are evaluable for the Month 12 study success criterion," At the time that approximately 50% of the patients were evaluable for the success criterion, the study enrollment was almost completd, and the sponsor decided not to conduct the administratieve futility analysis.

container_path: 9.7. Statistical Methods Planned in the Protocol and Determination of Sample Size

blocks.text:
For each safety analysis in which the outcome is an event (possibly composite), treatment groups were compared using counts and percentages.

Only treatment-emergent AEs were analyzed. AEs were coded using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 17. The number and percentage of patients with at least one adverse event, at least one serious adverse event (SAE), and at least one procedure related adverse event were presented by treatment group. The number and percentage of patients with at least one NeoCart related adverse event were presented for the NeoCart treatment group. AEs that are definitely, probably, or possibly related to the procedure, or for which the relationship to the procedure is missing, were considered procedure related, and AEs that are definitely, probably, or possibly related to NeoCart, or for which the relationship to NeoCart is missing, were considered NeoCart related. AEs and SAEs are summarized at the patient level by MedDRA system organ class (SOC) and preferred term using frequencies and percentages. AEs will also be tabulated at the event level by severity and by relationship to the procedure for each treatment group, and by relationship to NeoCart for the NeoCart treatment group.

All Adverse Events were captured during the study independent of relatedness to the treatment arm or procedure. Events were assessed by the principal investigator for causality and relatedness to either the procedure or the implant or both. Summaries were restricted to Treatment Emergent Adverse Events (TEAEs), which were defined as those AEs that occurred after the start of the arthroscopic procedure or worsened during the study. Verbatim terms were mapped to preferred terms and System Organ Classes using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) dictionary (version 17.

The key revisions to Protocol # 8-01 and the SAP are summarized below. As well, the Informed Consent Form and the Summary of Procedure Requirements were revised for consistency with the Protocol. A detailed summary of changes by protocol section is attached.

Histogenics is proposing revisions to the protocol to improve the study based on feedback from clinical sites to optimize patient enrollment and clarify protocol interpretation and compliance.

· Increase in the number of clinical sites from 30 to 40 for added availability of patients and patient flow

· Clarifications to inclusion/exclusion criteria to help clinical sites interpret and comply with protocol requirements

· Assessment and documentation of patient rehabilitation

· Clarifications to study stopping criteria for consistency with literature sources (note: no changes to rates or number of events as approved in Version 5 of the protocol)

· Clarify and add to risk analysis an option for either second biopsy or conventional treatment in the event of a manufacturing process failure or defect site increasing in size between arthroscopy and implantation (informed consent template revised to reflect same)

In addition to the proposed revisions to the protocol, Histogenics is also submitting a detailed statistical analysis plan (SAP) for the NeoCart Phase III Protocol #8-01. The proposed SAP was developed in accordance with the document entitled "NeoCart Trial Design Statistical Considerations", authored by Berry Consultants, LLC, dated March 1, 2010 and submitted to FDA as part of the SPA protocol.

The comprehensive SAP included with this protocol revision provides details and clarification to the above referenced Statistical Considerations document. There has been no change in the primary Month 12 efficacy endpoint and no change in the essential aspects of the analysis plan to be used to test for superiority. The key proposed revisions include the following:

· In addition to the KOOS and IKDC subjective score improvement criteria, the clinical composite success (CCS) criteria for Month 24 and Month 36 will require that the patient has not undergone a secondary re-operation for a failed index treatment to insure KOOS and IKDC scores are not reflecting successful secondary treatment for a primary treatment failure

· Details of the specific type of multiple imputation methodology to be used in sensitivity analyses of the primary superiority (Month 12) comparison

· Addition of a formal futility analysis based on conditional power to the previously specified administrative analysis. This futility analysis will be performed when 50% of the initial sample size is theoretically due for Month 12 follow-up.
