Key changes to Protocol # 8-01 are summarized below and a detailed summary table of changes by protocol section is attached. To allow for administrative efficiency, the Informed Consent Form (ICF) and the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) have been removed as attachments to the protocol.

Histogenics is proposing revisions to the protocol to improve the study based on feedback from clinical sites and Histogenics' DSMB. As well, changes have been made to collect additional health outcomes data and the statistical plan has been revised to address patients for whom the NeoCart implant is not available.

· Clarifications to prior surgical treatment of the study defect that are allowed and defining wash- outs for other surgical procedures.

· Modifications to the postoperative therapy regimen to both standardize treatment in both arms of the study and to further reduce risk factors for DVT/PE and arthrofibrosis in patients immobilized post-operatively.

o The use of a knee immobilizer is no longer a requirement for patients receiving NeoCart. Investigator discretion allowed for post-operative knee immobilization for both treatment groups.

o For patients not placed in a knee immobilizer, CPM will begin on the day of the study procedure. For patients that are placed in a knee immobilizer, CPM may begin as early as the day of the study procedure but, in any case, no later than the first post-operative visit.

o For any patient that is placed into a knee immobilizer following the study procedure, aspirin and TED hose will be ordered for, at a minimum, the duration of the immobilization period.

· Additional PRO health outcomes surveys (Marx Activity Rating Scale, SF-12, EQ-5D-5L, and WPAI) to potentially demonstrate improved Quality of Life (QOL) outcomes for patients, as well as NeoCart cost-effectiveness.

· Analysis population redefined to modified Intent-to-treat (mITT) patient population to include all patients randomized, except patients randomized to the NeoCart group for whom the NeoCart implant was not available. The primary efficacy analysis for the superiority claim will be based on the mITT population.

To date, four patients randomized to the NeoCart group did not receive the NeoCart due to various manufacturing-related issues (particulates, voluntary study suspension and failed lot release testing). Since the lack of NeoCart availability is not considered a negative reflection on the efficacy of actual treatment with NeoCart, it is thought that these patients should not be included in the efficacy analyses.

A total of 518 patients were consented; of these 269 were determined to be screen fails. A total of 148 patients were identified prior to the diagnostic procedure with 9.8% not meeting the inclusion criteria and 18.7% having one or more exclusion criteria. A total of 53 patients were excluded at the time of arthroscopy with 5.2% not meeting the inclusion criteria and another 5% having one or more exclusion criteria. There was a total of 33 sites that enrolled patients (30 in the US and 3f in Canada), 19 sites enrolled 5 or more patients in the study (see Table 10 for an accounting of the factors that contributed to screen failures). Thus, 249 patients entered the study and were randomized to either the treatmenttest or control arm, with 170 Randomized NeoCart patients, and 79 Microfracture patients, which constitute the Intent to Treat (ITT) study population. During the final stages of enrollment, the sponsor enrolled four (4) additional patients than anticipated due to the moderate screen failure rate. Patients who had already consented once 245 patients were enrolled were still allowed to proceed to be enrolled, if eligible in the final week of enrollment which took place in June 2017.

Table 8 details the patient accountability for patients enrolled in the study. Of the 249 patients who were randomized in the study (the ITT population), 235 patients completed their 1 year follow-up (235/249 = 94.4% retention rate); if one considers those patients that received treatment initially (the mITT population), then the overall 1-year retention rate was 97.1% (235/242). 10.3. Demographics and Baseline Characteristics
10.3.1. Demographics

Summaries of subject demographic and baseline disease characteristics are provided in Table 12 and Table 13 for the ITT and mITT populations, respectively. The study inclusion and exclusion criteria were chosen in agreement with the FDA to select for a subject population that would minimize bias against microfracture, the control procedure, where limitations are known in clinical practice. There were no appreciable differences betweenimputat the patients in each arm of the study. Of the 249 treated patients 66.05% in the NeoCart group and 60.0% in the microfracture arm were male. The mean age in the NeoCart group was 38.6 years and 38.9 in the microfracture group. The majority of patients categorized themselves as white (83.3% NeoCart/80.0% microfracture) with the next largest category Bblack or African American 8.6% NeoCart and 8.8% microfracture). Patients weighed between 105 and 286 pounds.

Baseline characteristics were generally balanced between the treatment groups. The mean age is 38.8 years and identical for the ITT population in both treatment arms. The mean lesion size was 2.4cm2 in the NeoCart arm and 2.1cm2 in the microfracture arm. The distribution between right and left knee for the index procedure was similar both between sides and treatment groups. There were slightly more Medial Femoral Condyle lesions in the NeoCart group (62.4%) than microfracture (48.1%). The mean age of injury NeoCart 1.94 years and microfracture 2.42 years

Table 14.1.9.1

Results from the arthroscopic evaluation for patients in both study arms within the ITT population are presented in Table 17.

The majority of patients had a single study lesion in the index knee (NeoCart 84.1%, microfracture 91.1%). The most common additional procedure performed was partial meniscectomy (24.7% NeoCart and 26.6% microfracture). The median % of meniscus remaining in both arms was 90%. The arthroscopic evaluation results for the mITT, AT, and PP populations are located in Appendix.

Prior surgical history of the index knee with either meniscal or ligament repair had occurred in 30% of the NeoCart patients and 33% of the microfracture patients.

There was no evidence of osteoarthritis in the overwhelming majority of the patients in either group and no impairment of the joint space or sclerosis. Both treatment groups demonstrated a normal varus axis alignment within 2-3 degrees of the mechanical axis of the treatment knee (NeoCart 52.9%, microfracture 54.4%) with approximately a third in each arm having minor valgus alignment.

The NeoCart implant characteristics are detailed in Table 20 for the AT population. In 89% of the cases, the surgeons reported complete contact of the implant with the native cartilage; 11% had a gap at the border that did not exceed 1 mm. In 94% of the cases, healthy cartilage was said to have surrounded the implant. The implant was rarely reported to be higher than the native cartilage. In general, the implant was found to be either the same height as the native cartilage or lower than the native cartilage (instances where "all" the implant was lower than the native cartilage occurred in 19/162 =12% of the cases). The NeoCart implant characteristics for the ITT, mITT, and PP populations are located in Section 14.1.4, Table 14.1.11.3.2, Table 14.1.11.3.3, and Table 14.1.11.3.4, respectively.

The baseline medical history of the ITT population is shown in Table 22. Overall, approximately two-thirds of the patients reported a history of "Musculoskeletal" conditions while one-third reported "Immunological" conditions. Smoking has been identified as a negative predictor for poor wound healing in general and specifically to be a negative influence on knee ligament and cartilage repair. (cite Kanneganti P et al, The effect of smoking on ligament and cartilage surgery in the knee: a systematic review, AJSM 2012, Dec: 40(12): 2872-2878.) The baseline smoking status of each arm within the ITT population is shown in Table 23. In the NeoCart arm, 8.2% of patients reported as current smokers/tobacco users; the balance either never smoked (77.6%) or were past smokers (14.1%). In the Microfracture arm, 5.1% of patients self-reported as current smokers/tobacco users, with the balance having never smoked (81.0%) or as previous smokers (13.9%). The baseline smoking status for the mITT, AT, and PP populations are located in Appendix.

blocks.text:
The primary endpoint for the Phase III study was defined as a test of superiority (one-sided Pearson's chi-square test, a =0.025) vs microfracture, in terms of a composite clinical success (CCS) used in a dual threshold responder analysis for pain and function at 1 year post index surgery. A subject was considered a responder if they achieved both of the following outcomes:

· An improvement of at least 12 points in outcome compared to baseline on the KOOS pain assessment test, and

· An improvement of at least 20 points in outcome compared to baseline on the IKDC subjective test.

The following tables (24, 25) detail the primary endpoint results for the different analysis groups with the difference in both percentage and statistical evaluations using the discussed analyses. The SAP specified the Pearson's Asymptotic P value (chi-square) where for the single sided superiority test statistical significance was almost reached in the ITT population (P=0.0744) and for those patients who actually received the NeoCart implant in the mITT population the results of improvement over microfracture was highly statistically significant (P=0.0257)

blocks.text: Post-hoc analyses were conducted to determine patient populations where certain meaningful improvements or statistically significant superiority results were identified, particularly where microfracture is known to have certain limitations or variability in success, such as in heavier patients, or those with larger lesions. These analyses were all conducted with prospectively collected data. The same data that was used to calculate the dual threshold responder rates.

blocks.text: 11.1.2.1. Lesion size
container_path: 11.1. Analyses of the primary efficacy variable

blocks.text:
With regard to lesion size, the NeoCart arm performed similarly across the entire study population (Table 26). However, there was a clear differentiation of microfracture in smaller lesion sizes only, with NeoCart showing statisticially significant superiority in lesions greater than 2.2 cm2 for the ITT population and greater than 1.6 cm2 for the mITT population. The mean lesion size for the study was 2.2 cm2, and for all lesions greater than that, NeoCart patients had a composite success rate of 71.7.% while the microfracture success rate was only 51.5% (p=0.0050) at 1 year for the ITT population. Evaluation of the earlier timepoint of 6 months demonstrated potential earlier pain relief and functional improvements, for lesions greater than 1.8 cm2 in the NeoCart arm. , At 6 months, NeoCart patients had a composite success rate of 59.5% while the microfracture success rate was only 40.5% (p=0.0177) at 1 year for the ITT population.

Similar to the relative performance in lesion sizes between NeoCart and microfracture, literature suggests that patient who have increased BMI demonstrate worse results with microfracture. Tables X & Y illustrate the impact of weight (BMI) on the 1-year primary efficacy endpoint with NeoCart performing equally across the different weight categories with a highly statistically significant improvement when compared to microfracture for those patients with a BMI of 28 or more. As noted above, microfracture is known to perform better in lower weight and younger patients. This has relevance in the United States as a BMI of greater than 24.9 is considered obese. Clinicians must take into account the limitations of a treatment that is impacted by weight in such a negative fashion, and regularly exclude such patients from receiving microfracture in their clinical practice.

In an effort to better understand if there was a specific lesion size cut-off where NeoCart and MF performed equally well below the mean lesion size of 2.2cm2 the data was analyzed in 0.2cm2 increments and is presented in Table 26. For the ITT population statistical significance of superiority of the NeoCart arm is reached at the 2.2cm lesion size. In the mITT population which represents those patients who actually received the NeoCart treatment there is a high degree of statistical superiority across all lesion sizes.

blocks.text: For Treatment failures the percentage was very low and equal between the two treatment arms with 4 patients in the NeoCart arm and 2 patients in the microfracture arm resulting in identical rates of 2.5% and a p value of < 0.9709. The Phase III trial also demonstrated several additional findings when reviewing those patients who demonstrated declines in pain and function scores following surgery. There were a few patients that did not respond favorably in both treatment arms. There was a very large difference between the treatment arms who reported worse outcomes after the procedure with 12.7% of microfracture compared to 2.5% in the NeoCart arm on the IKDC function scales. MRIs were obtained at the timepoints noted in Table 4 (Baseline, 6months, 1 year and then annually. The baseline MRI included the following views: Both legs, standing, full extension from femoral head to tibial malleolus, anterio-posterior, 45º flexion, weight bearing, postero- anterior and merchant view-30° flexion. The post procedure exam was a standard MRI and time for 63% of transverse relaxation read (T2) image acquisition to be performed at sites where T2 software was available.

All MRI images were submitted to the MRI Core Laboratory. Analysis included standard MRI review to assess the quality of the NeoCart implant and microfracture during the course of the
container_path: 11.2. Analyses of the secondary efficacy variables

blocks.text:
Clinical Study Report Study 8-01

trial. These MRI findings were divided into anatomic assessments that were made using generally accepted, well-established MRI sequences and more advanced sequences that allowed for the direct, qualitative assessment of both the area of NeoCart implant or microfracture.

In addition to standard MRI review, an advanced T2 mapping MRI sequence was obtained to evaluate for qualitative and quantitative assessment of the collagen component of the extracellular matrix of the NeoCart implant and adjacent articular cartilage. Standard MRI sequences provided high contrast between fat suppressed bone and cartilage; however, they are generally not fluid sensitive and are degraded in the postoperative setting due to susceptibility artifact. Fast spin echo sequences with high in-plane resolution provide good cartilage to fluid contrast, making them more sensitive to partial thickness lesions.

T2 relaxation time is a reproducible MRI parameter that reflects the internuclear reaction, or dephasing, that occurs as a result of transverse relaxation of the excited hydrogen dipoles. The stratification of T2 reflects the arrangement of the type II collagen fibers within the matrix. T2 mapping of articular cartilage at clinical field strengths reflects collagen fiber. Standardized regions of interest T2 mapping analysis was performed in the basilar and superficial halves of the area of NeoCart implant or microfracture, comparing this to T2 values in the adjacent cartilage that appears normal on standardized fast spin echo techniques. Particular attention was paid to the presence or absence of the zonal stratification of T2 of the area of the NeoCart implant or microfracture compared to the patient's native hyaline cartilage. This allowed the Core Lab to possibly determine whether the NeoCart implant formed repair cartilage with collagen orientation and T2 values similar to hyaline cartilage and the nature of the cartilage that formed as the result of the microfracture procedure.

At one year the MRI imaging results were similar between the two treatment arms with slightly more lesions being graded isointense in the NeoCart arm than the microfracture arm (37.5% vs 24.7%) and slightly more lesions being graded hypointense in the microfracture arm 27.2% vs 15.8%). Integration of the defect area was similar as well as the percentage with 67-100% fill (58.7 % NeoCart and 54.3% microfracture). Both groups had minimal hypertrophy, displacement, subchondral edema and similar scoring of bony overgrowth.

While T2 mapping has been thought to help determine the progression to mature hyaline cartilage there were no statistically significant differences in the relaxation time means for the superficial or deep layers or their standard deviations. The relaxation times at 6 months for the superficial cartilage was similar between treatment arms (62.5077msec NeoCart, 62.9531msec microfracture p=0.8191) The deep layer showed longer times for NeoCart while not statistically significant (57.4107 NeoCart vs 54.9544 msec microfracture p=0.2212). The one-year data showed a slight decrease in the relaxation times as would be expected for organizing tissue but there was no difference between the groups, and both were about 10msec longer than the normal tissue. Similar results were seen in the smaller Phase II study. Thus, for the NeoCart phase III clinical study MRI including T2 mapping provided minimal additional insigh into the healing process.

KOOS and IKDC scoring systems are validated methods of evaluating the success of treatment for knee pain. The FDA guidance document on clinical trial for treatment of knee cartilage recognizes the need to evaluate improvement in pain and physical function and the requirement to use at least two validated measures as no one instrument is sufficient. The raw data to determine the dual threshold responder analysis comes directly from the prospectively collected data individual subscales of KOOS and IKDC, as change from baseline for NeoCart versus microfracture treatment. These de-coupled scores provide a more a holistic view of a variety of patient outcomes. On most of these measures, a statistically significant improvement versus microfracture at one year was observed. The results for Years 1 for all KOOS subscales and IKDC subscale are shown in Figure 1. The individual results show statistically significant improvement in the NeoCart arm across all KOOS measures to the p ≤ 0.050 level.

In addition to the previously provided subjective pain and function measurements in the IKDC and KOOS subscales, the Company also collected data including VAS pain, Marx Activity Rating Scale, SF-12 Health Survey, EQ-5D-5L Health Questionnaire, WPAI Questionnaire, and other medications/drug therapies. The majority of the analyses of these patient reported outcome measures did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference between the two treatment groups.

SF-12 Health Survey: This is a 12 question validated survey that provides insight into the mental and physicial functioning and overall health related quality of life. Patients in both arms of the study had improved scores in the physical functioning score with a mean improvement from baseline for the NeoCart arm 15.7 points and 11.3 for microfracture meeting statistical significance p=0.0057. (table 14.2.4.3.2) For the physical component the mean change from baseline for the NeoCart group was 14.4 points and microfracture 11.8 with a trend towards significance (p=0.097). (table 14.2.4.1.2). Statistical significance was also reached for the Vitality scores at 1 year P=0.0332) Interestingly there was statistically significant improvement at the 6 month visit for bodily pain (p=0.0096), Social functioning (p=0.0049) and Emotional scores (p=0.0326). There was no difference in the general health or the mental component summary scores between the two treatment arms ( table 14.2.4.5.2 and 14.2.4.10.2)
Marx Activity Rating Scale:

a patient reported outcome measure that focuses on four activity points: running, deceleration, cutting and pivoting. There was no statistical difference between the two study arms and scores actually decreased because the test asks about activity for the preceding 12 months. Thus the period from baseline thought rehabilitation and recovery would be expected to demonstrate a decrease of activity.

EQ-5D-5L Health Questionnaire: There was a highly statistically significant improvement for NeoCart compared to microfracture at all time points for pain and discomfort scores over time (p=0.0066 at 3 months, 0.0053 at 6 months and p=0.0201 at 1 year). For usual activities statistically significant improvement for NeoCart was seen at 1 year (p=0.0482). There was no difference for the anxiety-depression scores at 1 year.

The Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI) Questionnaire is an instrument used to measure how impaired an individual may be due to a specific condition. It is also used to compare work impairments between treatment groups in clinical studies. For the NeoCart Phase III trial both treatment groups had similar baseline and 3-month scores. At 6 months and 1 year more patients reported less impairment in the NeoCart treatment arm (<25% impairment reported in 79.9% of the NeoCart group and 67.7% of the microfracture group.

The study also measured the use concomitant medications and separated out those medications that are classified as used for pain. Patients were asked to record pain medication within the last seven days prior to their clinic visit. There was a 19% decrease in the pain medication use at 6 months between the NeoCart and the microfracture treated patients and a 10% decrease at the one-year primary endpoint visit. These data reinforce the survey data from the VAS pain scale noted above.

The VAS pain scale demonstrated a meaningful trend towards decreased pain in the NeoCart arm, with the magnitude of the trend increased at each clinic visit while not reaching statistical significance. (P=0.9703 at 6 months and P= 0.0590 at 1 year). Despite the difference in pain there were no statistically significant differences in mobility, self-care, anxiety and depression.

For the various component scores fo the SF-12 questionairres there were statistical improvements of NeoCart over microfracture at 1 year in the ITT population for physical functioning (p=0.0057) and vitality (p=0.0332) with either no difference or slight trend towards improvement in the other scores but nothing statistically significant.

11.4. Efficacy Conclusions

NeoCart did not demonstrate statistically superior performance with the dual threshold responder analysis missing by approximately 2 patients. However, when the data is reviewed a number of very important conclusions can be drawn. First that for the independent scores of KOOS pain and IKDC NeoCart does demonstrate a clinically and statistically significance at both the 6m and 1 year time points. In addition, when the data is stratified by lesion size the performance separation is apparent at low lesion sizes and continues as lesion sizes increase. The primary endpoint for the Phase 3 clinical trial was a dual-threshold responder analysis measuring the improvement in KOOS pain and IKDC function scores for each patient treated with NeoCart compared to those treated with microfracture one year after the time of treatment. In clinical trials a threshold response is a way to take a continuous primary efficacy measure and dichotomize it into responders and non-responders. The threshold is set based upon expectations for what a clinically meaningful result would be. In a dual threshold endpoint, the subjects must meet the value set as a responder both of two different measurements to be considered a responder (often termed a super superiority trial). At the time of the NeoCart phase 3 clinical trial design and discussion with the agency for the special protocol assessment (SPA) there was limited data available regarding what was a clinically meaningful change from baseline for either KOOS or IKDC and there had not been any completed prospective randomized trials. As the field has evolved, clinicians have worked hard to identify the scores at which meaningful benefit can be determined. The current scores for IKDC starts at a 6-point improvement as early as 6 months and increases to around 15 or 16 points at later timeframes. For KOOS pain the meaningful clinically important difference is seen in the 8 to 10-point range. Both thresholds in

The NeoCart efficacy results from the pivotal study are clinically meaningful and relevant and should be put into the context of how the field of treatment for knee cartilage defects has evolved over the past 10 years since the NeoCart trial was designed. The NeoCart treatment group demonstrates a statistically significant improvement using the dual-threshold responder criteria at 6 months and continues to improve numerically to the one-year primary endpoint (Table 24), although not meeting the prespecified statistical superiority p-value. 12. SAFETY EVALUATION
12.1. Extent of exposure

✕

The NeoCart implant is (Cultured Autologous Neo-Cartilage) tissue implant is a 3-dimensional, white, opalescent disc (6cm2 area, 1.5to 2.0mm thick) designed to treat symptomatic defects of the articular cartilage of the knee. Patients in the clinical trial undergo standard arthroscopy and if randomized to the NeoCart arm a biopsy of normal cartilage is obtained. This biopsy is then used to create the autologous cartilage graft that is placed into the defect at a second procedure approximately 8 weeks after the biopsy. Patients randomized to the control arm have the microfracture procedure performed at the time of arthroscopy and are exposed to a single operative procedure. NeoCart patients are required to undergo a mini-arthrotomy second procedure for preparation and placement of the graft into the defect. Patients in the NeoCart arm are exposed to the implant and an adhesive used to affix the implant. Safety data is collected for all patients in both arms of the study for the duration of three years post baseline entry into the study with the follow-up for patients in the NeoCart arm continued through three years post implantation.

There were 12 serious TEAEs in the NeoCart arm (6.8%) and 6 in the microfracture group (7.5%; Table 27). TEAEs were similarly equal in both arms and observed in 151 patients (445 events), (622% of the NeoCart population and 58.8% of the microfracture p=0.4808.

13. DISCUSSION AND OVERALL CONCLUSIONS
13.1. Discussion

Commented [AG66]: This is good, however we'll need to refresh/update once rest is built out.

NeoCart's clinical effectiveness was demonstrated through clinically meaningful and statistically significant treatment related improvements in pain and function at the 1-year timepoint versus the microfracture control arm.

These data were generated from the largest adequate and well-controlled Phase III clinical study to date in a U.S representative patient population with stringent inclusion/exclusion standards based on FDA's input. The efficacy of NeoCart was measured using validated and FDAaccepted instruments such as KOOS pain and IKDC function that that can be directly correlated to clinically relevant benefits for patients.

NeoCart's safety was also established, with TEAEs and TESAEs occurring in comparable rates in both arms of the study with no unexpected TEAEs or TESAEs. NeoCart has a positive benefit/risk profile in the knee cartilage defect space, where treatment options are limited to treat pain and loss of function

The Phase 3 Clinical Trial of NeoCart did not meet the primary endpoint of a statistically significant superiority in pain and function in a dual threshold responder analysis 1 year after treatment as compared to microfracture. (Show table 14.2.11 Primary efficacy endpoint ITT population). However this failure to reach statistical significance in no way diminishes the facts that NeoCart provides a better alternative for the treatment of focal cartilage defects in the knee than current standard procedures. In the Phase III clinical trial the NeoCart treatment arm performed better than anticipated based upon what was predicted from the results of the Phase II clinical trial and in the statistical plan (74% success compared to 70% anticipated). Microfracture performed worse than NeoCart but better than was anticipated based upon the Phase II clinical results, what has been observed in clinical practice and what was in the statistical plan (62% vs the expected 50%). Thus, the pre-specified difference of approximately 15-20% was not attained and a statistically significant result for the total population was just missed (p=0.074 Pearson's chi-square for the ITT population and p=0.0257 for the mITT population).

The NeoCart efficacy results from the pivotal study are clinically meaningful and relevant and should be put into the context of how the field of treatment for knee cartilage defects has evolved over the past 10 years since the NeoCart trial was designed. The NeoCart treatment group demonstrates a statistically significant improvement using the dual-threshold responder criteria at 6 months and continues to improve numerically to the one-year primary endpoint mark (Table 4), although not meeting the prespecified statistical superiority p-value. NeoCart treatment also demonstrated improvement with statistically significance over the microfracture group for the majority of both the KOOS and IKDC subgroup analyses when measured independently as reflected in current FDA Guidance. The early benefit of the NeoCart arm is across all treatment

groups and is sustained through the 1-year primary endpoint further reinforcing the durability of replacing a cartilage defect with a predictable cartilage tissue construct as opposed to chondrocytes. In addition, from a "do no harm" perspective it is important to evaluate the safety performance of those patients who not only had positive results even if they did not meet the dual threshold responder criteria but those who appeared to respond poorly after treatment.

There are two previously FDA cleared or approved products for knee cartilage injuries (Carticel and MACI). Both products harvest healthy cartilage and then amplify the cells and return them to the area of the cartilage defect, Carticel as a cell suspension and MACI as a cell suspension seeded on a porcine collagen membrane. Carticel is no longer on the US market. There are fundamental differences between NeoCart and MACI product characteristics that may show distinct clinical advantages over time. NeoCart is a more mature cartilage tissue graft when it is implanted into the patient, rather than cells laid upon a collagen membrane. This is thought to account for the faster and potentially greater durability in result for patients. The demographics of the NeoCart phase III clinical study were different from those studied in the MACI Phase III SUMMIT clinical study that limit the ability for a direct comparison between these products. The lower limit of lesion sizes for inclusion in the Summit trial was 3.0cm2 and the mean lesion size was 4.8cm2 whereas in the NeoCart study the mean lesion size was 2.2cm2 with lesions treated from 0.5cm2 to 6cm2. This is important as microfracture treatment effect is known to perform better in smaller lesion sizes.

The SUMMIT trial also reported on the KOOS subscales with the co-primary using the pain and function (sports and recreation subscale) at the two-year timepoint, versus the 1-year timepoint for NeoCart. Finally, the trial also allowed concomitant procedures (>30%) making it difficult to assign benefit to the primary cartilage defect repair in those patients and included previous microfracture treatments (>30%), which is known to result in poor subsequent outcomes and durability. The SUMMIT trial was conducted entirely in Europe with a 100% Caucasian demographic. The NeoCart Phase III study was conducted in the United States and Canada with almost 9% African American and almost 9% Hispanic patients which is more reflective of the U.S. population.

Since 2014, at least four Phase III or Pivotal clinical trials for knee cartilage have been initiated by other third parties to our knowledge based on publicly available information. One trial (NOVOCART) is being conducted under an IND as a biologic or combination product, and the other three products (Hyalofast, GelrinC, Agili-C) are medical devices in clinical studies being performed under IDEs. All of these trials appear to have similar pain and function primary endpoints using measures of KOOS and/or IKDC either individually or as co-primary endpoints, designed as superiority trials with microfacture as the active control, or more recently a historical control arm, with 2-year endpoints, and a three year follow up period.

Unlike the MACI trial, these trials also suggest that previous microfracture or other invasive surgeries should be excluded along with concomitant procedures and be limited to smaller lesions such as in the NeoCart trials. We also understand from publicly available information that each of these trials have had substantial difficulty in enrolling patients, similar to the sponsor's lengthy experience. The narrow inclusion/exclusion criteria as seen in the NeoCart study, as well as public perceptions regarding the utility and efficacy of microfracture, have continued to make these trials both financially and logistically challenging.

There were a few patients that did not respond favorably in both treatment arms. From a "do no harm" perspective it is important to evaluate the safety performance of those patients who not only had positive results even if they did not meet the dual threshold responder criteria but those who appeared to respond poorly after treatment. There was a very large difference between the treatment arms who reported worse outcomes after the procedure with 12.7% of microfracture compared to 2.5% in the NeoCart arm on the IKDC function scales. Getting patients back to good functional performance is key both from a quality of life point of view and an ability to perform daily activities including driving a car, climbing stairs and being able to work. When evaluating the risk/benefit of the procedures there are several elements that demonstrate that the NeoCart procedure is unique to other knee cartilage repair options and are supported by the data. These are elective procedures with the overall goal of decreasing pain and improving the functional status of patients. The potential to impact long term function and decrease the progression to osteoarthritis and reduce the need for joint replacement surgery remains to be seen but has never been demonstrated with the alternative therapy of microfracture due to the eventual failure rate over time (Solheim, 2018). The process of taking a patient's own cartilage and amplifying it within a scaffold under the conditions present in the knee joint prior to implanting the tissue results in the differentiation of the cartilage cells to the optimum articular cartilage. This is further evidenced by the evaluation of articular hyaline cartilage biomarkers prior to release of the implant. Patients treated with NeoCart demonstrated a statistically significant faster recovery at 6 months post index procedure that is durable and continues to improve through up to the two years for which data is available.

In summary, based on our review of publicly available information regarding current standards, we believe the NeoCart Phase III study meets the FDA's current guidance in terms of conduct, patient demographics and inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the pain and function endpoints as chosen are appropriate to demonstrate efficacy and safety of an investigational treatment for knee cartilage injury.
13.2. Overall conclusion

In conclusion, NeoCart's clinical effectiveness was demonstrated through clinically meaningful and statistically significant treatment related improvements in pain and function at the 1-year timepoint versus the microfracture control arm. The data become even more powerful as lesion size increases above the 2.0cm2 size. While the limited application of Microfracture in larger lesions has been recognized this is the first study to clearly define the lesion size above which the risk of even intermediate term (1-year) may be too great for physicians and patients to accept. NeoCart offers a durable and safe option. The NeoCart phase 3 clinical study results demonstrate clinical benefit with a very acceptable risk profile. The ability to get patients back on their feet in half the time has demonstrable advantages from a health economics perspective, particularly in a broad range of lesions where microfracture is most often used, not in limited populations where it is no longer used.

blocks.text:
Patient 03-002 (NeoCart):

Event 1: Patient experienced Arthralgia that was first reported January 1, 2011, approximately 5 months after implantation on August 13, 2010.The patient was diagnosed with Chondral Degeneration (MedDra Cartilage Atrophy) at arthroscopy on October 12, 2012, at which time chondroplasty of a flap tear adjacent to the NeoCart implant, as well as approximately 50% of the NeoCart implant, was performed. Following the procedure, the patient reported immediate relief of pain. The Investigator assessed the event of Arthralgia as severe in severity and possibly related to both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure.

Event 2: On December 20, 2012, the patient was hospitalized for a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the non-study leg. The patient underwent an operation to fixate a fractured femur and irrigate and debride the wound. The patient was discharged on December 23, 2012 in stable condition. The Investigator assessed the event of Gun Shot Wound as severe in severity and unrelated to both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure.

The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on September 18, 2013.

Patient 03-005 (NeoCart):

Event 1: Patient suffered a Meniscus Injury (left medial meniscus tear) in the target knee on August 8, 2010, after randomization/biopsy, but prior to the implantation procedure. The Investigator assessed the event of Meniscus Injury as severe in severity and unrelated to both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure. During the index implantation procedure on September 10, 2010, the medial meniscus tear was repaired.
container_path: 14.3.3. Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events

blocks.text:
Event 2: On September 20, 2010, the patient was hospitalized for shortness of breath and hemoptysis and was found to have a pulmonary embolism. The Investigator assessed the event of Pulmonary Embolism as life-threatening, severe in severity, possibly related to NeoCart and probably related to the NeoCart procedure. The patient was discharged on September 30, 2010 with no shortness of breath, prescriptions for coumadin and Lovenox, and instructions to follow- up with the primary care provider.

Event 3: On December 31, 2011, it was discovered that patient 03-005 suffered a Meniscus Injury (left medial meniscus tear) in the target knee. Meniscectomy was recommended, but to date no known intervention has been performed. The Investigator assessed the event of Meniscus Injury as medically significant, severe in severity, and unrelated to both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure.

The patient has not been seen since September 26, 2012, following the 2-year follow-up visit and is considered lost to 3-year follow-up.

Patient 05-001 (NeoCart):

Patient suffered a Vertebral Fracture due to an accidental fall on July 3, 2015. The patient was treated with narcotic analgesics, and underwent L2 kyphoplasty on August 20, 2015, resulting in full recovery. The Investigator assessed the event as moderate in severity and unrelated to both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure.

The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on September 22, 2015.

Patient 09-014 (NeoCart)

Patient implanted with NeoCart on May 3, 2016, was diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis on May 9, 2016. Patient was treated with anti-coagulant therapy. Follow-up by ultrasound and laboratory tests on August 1, 2016 confirmed resolution of the deep vein thrombosis. The Investigator assessed the event as moderate in severity, probably related to both the NeoCart implant and the NeoCart procedure.

The patient completed the 1 year follow up visit on June 8, 2017 and remains on study.
container_path: 14.3.3. Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events

blocks.text: Patient 10-003 (NeoCart):
container_path: 14.3.3. Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events

blocks.text:
Patient was diagnosed with Arthrofibrosis on October 22, 2014 after the patient failed to regain full range of motion of the target knee early after the implantation procedure. On November 11, 2014, the patient underwent adhesiolysis of the target knee and the event resolved. The Investigator assessed the event of Arthrofibrosis as moderate in severity, unlikely related to NeoCart, and definitely related to the NeoCart procedure.

The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on September 6, 2017.

Patient 13-003 (NeoCart):

Patient was diagnosed with Cholelithiasis on October 8, 2014. Cholecystectomy was performed on October 9, 2014. The Investigator assessed the event as life threatening, severe in severity, and unrelated to both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure.

The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on August 30, 2017.

Patient 17-003 (NeoCart):
container_path: 14.3.3. Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events

blocks.text:
Inefficient evacuation of bile Gallbladder, Removal/Cholecystectomy/Cholecystitis The patient had the NeoCart procedure.

Patient 21-001 (NeoCart):

Event 1: Patient was diagnosed with Arthrofibrosis on July 16, 2014 after the patient failed to regain full range of motion of the target knee early after the implantation procedure. On July 17, 2014, the patient underwent adhesiolysis of the target knee. The Investigator assessed the event of Arthrofibrosis as moderate in severity, unrelated to NeoCart, and definitely related to the NeoCart procedure.

Event 2: On September 22, 2014, the patient experienced a Lateral Meniscus Tear of the target knee. Partial meniscectomy was performed on December 22, 2014, resulting in resolution of associated symptoms. The Investigator assessed the event as unrelated to both NeoCart and the NeoCart procedure.

The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on June 27, 2017.

Patient 23-005 (NeoCart):

Event 1: Patient experienced Femoral Condyle Graft Failure (MedDRA Transplant Failure) approximately 6 months after implantation performed on January 26, 2016, and underwent re- operation for chondroplasty on July 26, 2016. The event was assessed by the Investigator to be severe in severity, definitely related to NeoCart, and possibly related to the NeoCart procedure.

Event 2: October 2, 2017, Patient 23-005 was evaluated for an abdominopelvic mass. She admitted with increased abdominal pain, girth and bloating. CT scan noted an abdominopelvic cystic mass on the left ovary measuring 17.1x28.4x24.3cm. The patient underwent left salpingo- oophorectomy on October 11, 2017. She was discharged on October 15, 2017 and instructed to follow-up with primary physician.
container_path: 14.3.3. Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events

blocks.text: Patient 33-003 (NeoCart)
container_path: 14.3.3. Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events

blocks.text:
Patient implanted with NeoCart on May 3, 2016, was diagnosed with Peptic Ulcer Hemorrhage on May 16, 2016. Patient underwent endoscopy and cauterization of the ulcer on May 18, 2016. Patient was found to have low hemoglobin levels and received 4 units of whole blood. Cause of ulcer is believed to be patient's concomitant use of aspirin with ibuprofen. Patient was discharged on May 19, 2016 and was asymptomatic as of follow up visit on May 27, 2016. The Investigator assessed the event as severe in severity, possibly related to the surgical procedure, and unlikely to be related to NeoCart implant.

The patient completed the 2 year follow up visit on May 2, 2018 and remains on study.

Patient 36-001 (NeoCart):

Patient suffered Deep Vein Thrombosis on January 11, 2016. The event was resolved March 3, 2016. The investigator assessed the event as severe in severity, unlikely related to NeoCart, and definitely related to the NeoCart procedure.

The patient completed the 2 year follow up visit on January 15, 2018 and remains on study.

Patient 36-005 (NeoCart)
container_path: 14.3.3. Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events

blocks.text:
Patient was diagnosed with ocular melanoma on March 2, 2017 and underwent treatment with an implantation of a radiation disc into his eye on March 13, 2017. The disc was explanted on March 17, 2017. The Investigator assessed the event as moderate in severity and unrelated to both NeoCart and NeoCart procedure.

The patient completed the 1 year follow up visit on February 22, 2018 and remains on study.

Patient 03-013 (Microfracture):

Patient was diagnosed with Increased Knee Pain and Failure of Microfracture Surgery on June 19, 2014 following the 2-year time point follow-up visit. On February 6, 2015, the patient underwent re-operation to remove damaged cartilage and perform osteochondral allografting.

The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on October 14, 2015.

Patient 03-027 (Microfracture):

Patient was diagnosed with attritional failure of microfracture (MedDRA PT Surgical Failure) following microfracture treatment performed on December 12, 2014 with persistent and increasing pain requiring re-operation. After nearly 2 years of conservative treatment, patient underwent reoperation of the index knee on August 4, 2016, at which time an osteochondral allograft procedure was performed. The Investigator assessed the event as severe in severity, and possibly related to the microfracture procedure.

The patient has not been seen since December 9, 2015, following the 1-year follow-up visit and is considered lost to follow-up.

Patient 13-009 (Microfracture)

Patient was diagnosed with appendicitis on October 23, 2016 and underwent appendectomy on October 25, 2016 with full resolution on October 26, 2016. The Investigator assessed the event as moderate in severity and unrelated to the microfracture procedure.

The patient completed the 2 year follow up visit on June 4, 2018 and remains on study.

Patient 23-003 (Microfracture):

Patient experienced Failure of Microfracture Surgery on May 26, 2015 (MedDRA PT Surgical Failure) after initial surgery on December 17, 2014. Patient underwent re-operation in April 2017 at which time osteochondral allografting was performed. The Investigator assessed the event as moderate in severity and definitely related to the microfracture procedure.

The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on October 18, 2017.

Patient 34-013 (Microfracture)

Patient developed C4-C5 cervical stenosis in July 2016. He was admitted and underwent spinal fusion surgery on July 27, 2017. The patient's post-operative course was complicated by a hematoma which prolonged the hospitalization. He underwent a re-operation on July 28, 2017 to remove the hematoma. These were reported as 2 separate serious events.

The patient completed the study at the 3-year follow-up visit on August 6, 2018.

Patient 41-003 (Microfracture):
container_path: 14.3.3. Deaths, other serious adverse events, and other significant adverse events

blocks.text:
Patient was diagnosed with Popliteal Artery Entrapment Syndrome on October 13, 2016. Popliteal artery release was performed on October 14, 2016, and the event was considered resolved at surgical follow-up on February 13, 2017. The Investigator assessed the event as moderate in severity and unrelated to the microfracture procedure.

The patient completed the 2 year follow up visit on May 1, 2018 and remains on study.
